# Reference Architecture {#sec-vol3-app-reference-architecture}

The chapters build an agent system one mechanism at a time, each where its failure first appears. This appendix assembles those mechanisms into a single reference architecture, so that a reader designing a system, reviewing one, or tracing a failure across it can check which components are present, what each one owns, which H·S·A exposure it closes, and which chapter derives it. It is organized by the components the book uses (the model, context and memory, tools and sandboxes, the harness, the durable log, recovery, evaluation, the learning loop, and the fleet) and names techniques rather than products; where an implementation is mentioned, it is one example of the technique.

## How to Use This Appendix {.unnumbered}

Consult the section that matches the question in front of you.

- **When you are designing a new agent system and need a checklist of components and the interfaces between them**, start with the component map in @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-mapping.
- **When a task's H·S·A position is known and you need to decide how much of the architecture it requires**, use the closure profiles in @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-profiles.
- **When a failure crosses components and you need to know which one owned the step that went wrong**, follow one turn through the architecture in @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-turn.
- **When you are choosing an isolation envelope and need representative start costs**, use @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-actuation.
- **When you are laying out where durable state lives and who may write it**, use @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-memory.
- **When you are deploying the architecture across machine pools and need the failure signals each pool emits**, use @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-blueprint, and classify the failure itself with @sec-vol3-app-failure-taxonomy.

## The Component Map {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-mapping}

An agent system has one component that proposes and many that decide. The model reads a context and returns a proposal (@sec-vol3-foundation-model). The surrounding components select what the model sees, mediate permitted effects, preserve state across stated failures, and gather evidence for acceptance. @Fig-vol3-agentic-architecture maps these responsibilities and the interfaces between them. @Tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-matrix expands the map into implementation responsibilities, the exposures they address, and failures that missing controls can permit.

| Component              | Owns                                                                                             | Exposure closed       | Invariant it enforces                                                                                      | Failure when absent                                                             | Chapter                       |
|:-----------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------|
| **Model service**      | The call surface, sampling, stop reasons, token accounting                                       | None (the origin)     | Every output is a proposal until the runtime acts on it                                                    | Proposals treated as results; fluent output taken as done                       | @sec-vol3-foundation-model    |
| **Context assembler**  | What each call sees: layout, provenance labels, compaction, invalidation                         | State ($S_1$)         | Every staged item has a source, a budget share, and a validity rule                                        | Context overflow, dilution, stale observations, poisoning                       | @sec-vol3-context-engineering |
| **Serving memory**     | Derived attention state, prefix reuse, residency during tool waits                               | State ($S_1$)         | Reuse requires compatible available state; reconstruction requires the inputs and compatible configuration | Memory stranded during tool waits; prefix reuse lost to layout churn            | @sec-vol3-kv-cache            |
| **Durable stores**     | Sources, agent-written memory, retrieval indexes, the retrieval contract                         | State ($S_3$)         | Authority stays with the source; every derived copy is checked against it                                  | Stale retrieval, self-written poisoning, contradictions with disk               | @sec-vol3-long-term-memory    |
| **Tool gateway**       | Schema validation, the grant, idempotency keys, settlement, observation shaping                  | Authority             | Complete mediation: no call reaches the environment without validation and a grant                         | Duplicate effects, unvalidated calls, unreadable observations                   | @sec-vol3-tool-calling        |
| **Isolation envelope** | Scoped grants, credential placement, workspace, egress, reset, and pools                         | Authority             | Enforced execution reach and lifetime under a stated threat model                                          | Running code reaching unintended resources or inheriting another tenant's state | @sec-vol3-sandboxes           |
| **Harness**            | The trajectory record, the state set, control actions, approval gates, budgets                   | Horizon               | The runtime can pause, bound, or stop the loop without the model's cooperation                             | Runaway loops, stale observations admitted, required approval bypassed          | @sec-vol3-agent-harness       |
| **Trajectory log**     | Write-ahead intent, checkpoints, resume, replay                                                  | Horizon               | No external effect leaves the host before the intent that authorizes it is durable                         | Lost progress after a crash; repeated effects on resume                         | @sec-vol3-durable-execution   |
| **Recovery**           | Sagas and compensation, the pivot boundary, forward repair, progress detection, circuit breakers | Horizon and Authority | Recovery templates and binding rules precede compensable dispatch; residual duties remain owned            | Half-finished effects, silent spinning, retry storms                            | @sec-vol3-failure-recovery    |
| **Evaluation**         | Task environments, grading, repeated-trial statistics, traces, attribution, release gates        | All three (measured)  | Acceptance follows declared criteria and scoped evidence, not activity signals                             | Releases gated on transcripts; failures blamed on the wrong layer               | @sec-vol3-evaluation          |
| **Learning loop**      | Curation, admission cascades, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning against verifiers              | No authority granted  | Training admission follows its intended use, evidence, and split policy                                    | Training on unverified or contaminated trajectories; reward hacking             | @sec-vol3-trajectory-curation |
| **Fleet**              | Multi-agent envelopes and delegation, capacity, routing, spending governance                     | All three multiplied  | Authority only attenuates on delegation; every accepted task has a price                                   | Correlated errors, orphaned work, budgets breached across delegation            | @sec-vol3-multi-agent         |

: **The Component Map**: Each component of an agent system, what it owns, the H·S·A exposure it closes, the invariant it enforces, the failure its absence produces, and the chapter that develops it. {#tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-matrix tbl-colwidths="[13,20,11,22,20,14]"}

The table reads in two directions. Read down the "Owns" column, it is a checklist, and a system that cannot name the component responsible for each row has a gap. Read across the "Failure when absent" column, it is a diagnostic, and a failure that matches a row points at the component that should have prevented it. Even the model service's invariant is enforced by the runtime rather than by the model, because every invariant in the table holds below the model (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}).

## Closure Profiles by Exposure {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-profiles}

Not every task needs every component. A read-only question-answering loop needs a context assembler and a harness with a turn ceiling, and adding a saga engine to it only adds cost. A production change needs nearly everything. The H·S·A position of a task (@sec-vol3-intro-hsa) decides how much of the architecture it requires, and @tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-profiles states the minimum for each level.

| Exposure level                               | Minimum closure the runtime supplies                                                                            | Components that must be present                    |
|:---------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|
| **Horizon, short** ($H \lesssim 10$)         | Turn, token, and cost ceilings; output ceiling and deadline on each call                                        | Harness (budgets)                                  |
| **Horizon, long** ($H \gtrsim 100$)          | Durable log with write-ahead intent, checkpoints, resume, progress detection                                    | Harness, trajectory log, recovery                  |
| **State $S_1$** (context only)               | A context budget, provenance labels, compaction that keeps identifiers verbatim                                 | Context assembler, serving memory                  |
| **State $S_2$** (sandboxed workspace)        | A workspace leased to the trajectory, reset between tenants, snapshots bound to log positions                   | Isolation envelope, trajectory log                 |
| **State $S_3$** (durable, shared)            | A retrieval contract that checks version and provenance against the source; a write path the runtime admits     | Durable stores, context assembler                  |
| **Authority $A_0$** (read)                   | Credentials kept out of context; egress restricted, since reading can still leak                                | Tool gateway, isolation envelope (egress)          |
| **Authority $A_1$** (sandboxed mutation)     | An envelope matched to the code, capabilities scoped to the workspace, a reset contract                         | Tool gateway, isolation envelope                   |
| **Authority $A_2$** (retriable, compensable) | Idempotency keys and settlement before retry; a compensator registered before dispatch                          | Tool gateway, trajectory log, recovery             |
| **Authority $A_3$** (irreversible)           | Current policy and action-time checks; approval where required, with expiry and revalidation; recovery ordering | Harness (approval gate), recovery (pivot boundary) |

: **Closure Profiles by Exposure Level**: The minimum closure the runtime must supply at each H·S·A level and the components that supply it. A task needs the union of the rows its position selects, and the evidence level of its completion criteria rises with the same exposure. {#tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-profiles tbl-colwidths="[22,50,28]"}

A task selects one row from each exposure and needs the union of what they require. The flaky-test repair of @sec-vol3-intro-workflow-vs-loop sits at a long horizon, $S_2$, and $A_1$, so it needs the harness, the trajectory log, recovery, the isolation envelope, and the tool gateway, with approval only where its task policy requires it. The same agent pushing its fix to a shared branch moves to $A_2$ for the push and $S_3$ for the branch, which adds settlement, a compensator, and a source check on anything it later retrieves about that branch. Lowering a task's authority to what it needs is usually cheaper than building closure for authority it never needed, which is the lesson of the incident in @sec-vol3-intro-hsa.

## One Turn Through the Architecture {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-turn}

A single turn of a long trajectory touches almost every component, and each step has one owner. Following the turn in order shows where each invariant is checked and which log event records it.

1. **Admit the turn.** The harness considers a `READY` trajectory, checks current grants and control state, and reserves the proposed bounded liability against actual consumption and existing reservations while preserving finalization resources. Admitted work moves to `CALLING_MODEL` (@sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine).
2. **Assemble the context.** The context assembler builds the call from the trajectory's history under the context budget, stable prefix first and volatile content last, with provenance labels on untrusted text (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging). The log records that the context was built, with a hash of what went in.
3. **Call the model.** The model service receives the call with an output ceiling and a deadline, reuses the cached prefix where it can (@sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree), and returns a proposal with a stop reason and token usage (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract). The log records the reply.
4. **Validate and grant.** The tool gateway validates the proposal and applies runtime policy to the session, target, operation, and current preconditions. A discovered descriptor does not confer permission (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-mcp). Calls requiring approval go to the approval gate before dispatch (@sec-vol3-controlplane-hitl).
5. **Write intent, then dispatch.** The trajectory log makes the intent durable under the declared storage failure domain before dispatch (@sec-vol3-persistence-wal). Where the workflow supplies a compensating operation, its recovery plan is recorded as well (@sec-vol3-sagas-architecture). The gateway dispatches under the task's enforced grant and execution limits, preserving a logical operation identity where the endpoint supports that retry contract (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-least-privilege, @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency).
6. **Wait without holding more than needed.** The harness moves the trajectory to `WAITING_TOOL`. The serving memory decides whether the trajectory's attention state stays resident, is evicted and recomputed, or is offloaded for the length of the wait (@sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping).
7. **Record the outcome and shape the observation.** The gateway correlates returning evidence with its call, preserving known results, partial effects, or unresolved status. Late outcomes can matter for reconciliation even when they should not resume the model. The log records this disposition and the bounded observation (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-streaming).
8. **Check progress and continue.** Recovery compares task-scoped observations with recent history to assess possible nonprogress (@sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs). The harness applies its guarded continuation or finalization decision. Evaluation assesses acceptance under the declared criteria, including any required residual-duty evidence; its final verdict need not be available when finalization begins (@sec-vol3-evaluation-contract).

Recorded spans correlate observed calls and outcomes (@sec-vol3-evaluation-tracing). Captured inputs may support replay tests, while controlled reruns test diagnostic hypotheses. Missing evidence and interacting causes limit attribution.

## The Model Service {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-processor}

The rest of the architecture needs five things from the model service, and none of them is the model's accuracy. It needs a typed call surface, so a finished tool call can be told from a truncated one and an answer from a refusal (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract). It needs stop reasons, because they are the loop's control signal. It needs token usage per call, because every budget in the harness is counted in tokens. It needs cancellation, so the harness can stop generation the moment a streamed proposal fails validation. And it needs prefix reuse across the turns of one trajectory, because a trajectory re-sends its context on every turn and prefix caching is the dominant saving on that re-sent input (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost).

Behind that surface, the serving system applies techniques whose effects an agent engineer sees directly. Paged allocation lets requests draw from one block pool and share compatible prefix state (@sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention). A prefix cache can avoid reconstructing a compatible prefix when its state remains available and sharing is permitted (@sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree). Batching amortizes shared work, while chunked prefill creates scheduling opportunities that can reduce interference with ongoing decode work; neither mechanism alone guarantees request latency (@sec-vol3-appendix-inference-roofline, @sec-vol3-kvcache-chunked-prefill). @Sec-vol3-appendix-inference-kv-cache derives the attention payload per token, and @sec-vol3-appendix-inference-queueing distinguishes resident capacity from service rate.

Two design consequences follow for the rest of the architecture. Routing all turns of a trajectory to a server that still holds its prefix turns most re-sent input into cache hits, so the harness and the fleet router should carry a session identifier that the serving layer can use for affinity. And any change to the stable prefix, such as reordering tool definitions or inserting a timestamp near the top of the context, silently discards that saving, so the context assembler owns cache stability as much as the serving layer does (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging).

## Context and Memory {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-memory}

An agent's state lives in several places that differ in who may write them, how long they last, and what maintains their validity. The architecture needs an owner for each, and it must distinguish a derived copy from its source (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}). @Tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-memory maps these responsibilities to components. The persistent-record roles in @tbl-vol3-memory-tiers further distinguish the claims and evidence retained in durable stores.

| State class              | Level | Component that owns it      | Who may write                                | Validity and maintenance contract                                        |
|:-------------------------|:-----:|:----------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Working context**      | $S_1$ | Context assembler           | Runtime assembles; the model only reads      | Rebuilt every turn; stale items invalidated against their source         |
| **Attention state**      | $S_1$ | Serving memory              | Serving engine, derived from tokens          | Recomputed from its token prefix when evicted                            |
| **Workspace artifacts**  | $S_2$ | Isolation envelope          | The agent, through tools, inside the sandbox | Leased per trajectory, reset between tenants, snapshotted at checkpoints |
| **Source artifacts**     | $S_3$ | The owning system           | Owners and granted tool writes               | Authoritative; change only through explicit writes                       |
| **Trajectory log**       | $S_3$ | Trajectory log              | Runtime only, append-only                    | Never rewritten; the trajectory record is folded from it                 |
| **Agent-written memory** | $S_3$ | Durable stores (write path) | The model proposes; the runtime admits       | Admission, correction, supersession, expiry, and deletion by policy      |
| **Retrieval indexes**    | $S_3$ | Durable stores (indexer)    | Indexer only, rebuilt from sources           | Invalidated when a source changes; disposable                            |

: **State Classes by Owner**: Where each class of agent state lives in the reference architecture, who may write it, and what keeps it consistent with the world. {#tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-memory tbl-colwidths="[18,7,20,25,30]"}

Three architectural rules follow from the table. First, a trajectory log records the events captured under its durability and retention contract; it does not establish every claim made in a logged response. Second, reconstruction requires retained inputs and a compatible reconstruction procedure. An index can be rebuilt from available sources, but a preference or observation cannot be recovered merely because an agent originally wrote it. Losing its only retained evidence can change later behavior. Third, the model proposes writes through mediated tools; workspace containment and memory admission enforce different boundaries on those operations. The context assembler selects from these records, and the retrieval contract (@sec-vol3-persistent-governance) governs how durable information re-enters a call, preserving its applicability, provenance, and retrieval limitations.

## Tools and Sandboxes {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-actuation}

The tool gateway mediates requests and returning evidence; the isolation envelope constrains execution reach. The gateway validates arguments, applies session policy and action-time checks, dispatches permitted calls, and returns bounded observations. Retry behavior depends on operation semantics and the endpoint's supported identity, effect, and result contract. A timeout may remain unresolved; a key alone does not make repetition safe (@sec-vol3-tool-calling). The envelope enforces the implementation's permitted resource access, credentials, workspace effects, network reach, and resource use (@sec-vol3-sandboxes). Neither a grant nor a descriptor enforces those limits merely by naming them.

Envelope choice depends on required interfaces, the threat model, and the configured enforcement boundary. @Tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-sandboxes summarizes the decision factors developed in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-envelope-choice; it does not assign universal timings or rank isolation strength by product name.

| Envelope                | Shared or trusted components                                                | Compatibility and resource questions                                                        |
|:------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Shared-kernel container | Host kernel and configured isolation controls                               | Which host interfaces, identities, mounts, and devices remain reachable?                    |
| User-space kernel       | Interposed application-kernel implementation and its host interface         | Does the toolchain use supported interfaces, and what does its actual I/O cost?             |
| MicroVM                 | Guest kernel, VMM/hypervisor boundary, configured devices and host services | What initialization, guest residency, I/O, and reset costs does the deployment incur?       |
| Restricted bytecode     | Execution runtime and exposed host imports                                  | Can the workload target this format, and are memory, execution, and import effects bounded? |

: **Envelope decision factors**: Startup, steady execution, residency, and teardown must be measured for the workload and configuration. Shared baseline memory is an implementation-dependent optimization, not a universal property of an envelope type. {#tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-sandboxes tbl-colwidths="[20,35,45]"}

Provisioning also depends on lifetime policy. A warm lease, a fresh restore, and a verified reset are different events. Pool capacity needs an explicit reserve, replenishment concurrency, admission policy, and memory ledger; average arrival rate alone does not establish that an environment is ready when needed (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling).

Supporting services enforce distinct boundaries. A credential broker withholds selected secrets from the guest and checks authorized use, while task data and returned observations may still be sensitive (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-credential-brokering). Egress controls constrain actual routes, destinations, and supported request semantics; permitted requests can still carry inappropriate disclosures (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-network). Security develops provenance and information-flow policy for those remaining cases (@sec-vol3-security-taint-tracking).

## The Harness {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-orchestration}

The harness owns the loop for one trajectory. Its central data structure is the trajectory record: identity, current state and version, per-call limits, budgets, actual and reserved consumption, grants and leases, pending work and unresolved effects, and references to context, plan, log, and workspace (@sec-vol3-controlplane-acb). The model never writes this control state directly. Guarded transitions separate eligibility to continue from ownership of effects. A late result cannot directly update an obsolete continuation, but authenticated, correlated evidence is retained for settlement. A held call is dispatched only after the applicable approval and current admission checks pass (@sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine).

Control requests are recorded independently of model output and applied through guarded lifecycle transitions (@sec-vol3-controlplane-signals). Pause holds continuation; resume rechecks current task conditions, grants, budget, and pending evidence. A call requiring approval remains undispatched until a current authorization and admission checks permit it, or denial or expiry resolves the hold (@sec-vol3-controlplane-hitl). Budgets govern further admission using actual consumption and reserved liability; stopping admission does not erase charges or effects already in flight (@sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting). Durable execution develops when another worker can reconstruct the record and safely continue it.

## The Durable Log and the Trace {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-observability}

The trajectory log preserves the runtime's recorded decisions and evidence. A fixed update function can reconstruct the selected record from a complete authoritative history and its required inputs (@sec-vol3-persistence-event-sourcing). Before dispatch, the runtime obtains the durable acknowledgment required by its declared failure domain for the intent and associated admission state. An incomplete replica's missing intent is not evidence that no request was sent (@sec-vol3-persistence-wal).

A checkpoint publishes compatible record, workspace, and artifact state at an exact log boundary only after its required constituents are durably available. Reconstruction applies the suffix to both the record and affected workspace state (@sec-vol3-persistence-checkpointing). Resume validates the authoritative history and artifacts, establishes current ownership, preserves unresolved operations and charges, and checks current authority and dependencies before admitting work (@sec-vol3-persistence-migration). Reconstructing recorded decisions differs from rerunning harness logic against captured inputs: a regression replay disables live effect paths and states which inputs and behavior it can reproduce (@sec-vol3-persistence-replay).

The trace serves measurement rather than recovery. It records instrumented spans and links, with capture coverage stated (@sec-vol3-evaluation-tracing). Its available attributes can include token counts, durations, and outcomes; sampling and redaction determine which diagnostic details survive. Recovery-required events and artifacts must remain complete and available for their declared recovery lifetime. Diagnostic copies may follow a different sampling and retention policy. One storage system can serve both purposes if it preserves those distinct requirements.

## Recovery {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-recovery}

The log supplies recorded evidence, including unresolved outcomes. Recovery chooses among permitted retries, bounded revised proposals, compensation, containment, and escalation (@sec-vol3-failure-recovery). A repair is new admitted work; comparing its expected cost with unwind requires the same target outcome and explicit fallback assumptions (@sec-vol3-sagas-forward-vs-backward). Compensation metadata precedes forward dispatch, while generated resource identities bind from adequate evidence afterward. Cleanup follows its dependency order and current authority, resource, and repeat contracts; unresolved outcomes retain an owner (@sec-vol3-sagas-architecture). Commitment regions state what cannot be undone, what partial outcomes are possible, and which duties remain, rather than imposing one irreversible action on every trajectory (@sec-vol3-sagas-pivot).

Watchdogs compare task-scoped observations to flag possible nonprogress; repeated hashes alone do not establish a useless loop (@sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs). Dependency-scoped breakers, coordinated safe retries, and bounded resource pools limit further load without canceling effects already forwarded (@sec-vol3-sagas-containment). Incident containment stops model-directed admission, preserves evidence and unresolved obligations, and can retain narrowly authorized independent cleanup. Suspect-artifact status follows affected versions and dependencies, not an assumption that every artifact is compromised (@sec-vol3-sagas-quarantine).

## Evaluation {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-evaluation}

Evaluation supplies a declared acceptance contract and comparable task fixtures (@sec-vol3-evaluation-gyms). Protected checks and calibrated judgments assess their stated criteria without becoming infallible (@sec-vol3-evaluation-grading). Statistical comparisons preserve the task and run units and any pairing, and distinguish candidate availability from repeated-run consistency (@sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor). Diagnosis combines available records, captured-input replay, and controlled new runs, reporting what their results support and leave unresolved (@sec-vol3-evaluation-postmortems). Offline, shadow, and canary stages answer different questions under explicit exposure and decision policies (@sec-vol3-evaluation-releases).

The evaluation environment can reuse isolation mechanisms and pools (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-substrate) under its declared fixture and threat model. Protect grading logic, credentials, and authoritative results from both the acting agent and candidate code executed during grading. Read-only test storage alone does not prevent in-process interference or disclosure. Separately scoped credentials, egress controls, and observation boundaries support the intended comparison; the report must still state which production behaviors the fixture omits.

## The Learning Loop {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-learning}

The learning loop uses evaluation evidence under a separate curation and training-admission contract. Curation determines which trajectories support the intended learning use, protects acceptance evidence, and separates training material from held-out assessment (@sec-vol3-trajectory-curation). Supervised fine-tuning serializes admitted trajectories into the model's call format and computes loss on the selected policy targets (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning). Reinforcement learning optimizes against verifiers protected from the policy's rollouts (@sec-vol3-rlvr).

The loop adds a collection and rollout workload whose capacity depends on the training experiment, a governed data path from recorded runs to versioned learning artifacts, and a release path back into the model service. Transformations and admission checks determine which records reach which consumer; the log itself is not the corpus. A changed policy may alter trajectory length, state use, and requested effects without acquiring additional authority. Its release therefore requires renewed behavioral evidence under the existing runtime bounds, not an assumption that training leaves the exposures unchanged.

## Deployment and the Fleet {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-blueprint}

A deployment separates the architecture into pools whose resources, failure modes, and security boundaries differ. The model service runs on accelerator nodes and is sized by attention-state memory and decode throughput. Harness workers are stateless, run on ordinary hosts, and are sized by the number of live trajectories. Sandbox hosts run the isolation envelopes with hardware virtualization, sit behind the egress proxy, and are never on the same network as the durable stores. The durable stores hold the trajectory log, the source systems' mirrors, agent-written memory, and retrieval indexes. Verification runs on hosts the agent's envelopes cannot reach.

Resources held throughout a trajectory depend on its lifetime, not merely the duration of one model call. Under stable flow, Little's law relates mean live trajectories to admitted arrival rate and mean lifetime (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-capacity; @sec-vol3-appendix-inference-queueing). That product is not a hard admission limit or a guarantee against reserve exhaustion: bursts, variability, outstanding work, and reclamation require additional accounting. Across agents, typed task envelopes carry scoped authority and budgets (@sec-vol3-multiagent-contracts), reservations account for concurrent spending (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-governance), and cancellation requires supervision of the work and effects it reaches (@sec-vol3-multiagent-backpressure).

Each pool fails in its own way and emits its own signal. @Tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-failures lists the signal to watch and the component that responds.

| Symptom                                              | Pool            | Likely cause                                                                    | Signal to watch                                                                                                              | Responding component and chapter                                                          |
|:-----------------------------------------------------|:----------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Calls queue while accelerators sit idle**          | Model service   | Attention state held by trajectories waiting on tools                           | Resident attention state per active decode stream                                                                            | Serving memory: evict, recompute, or offload during waits (@sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping)    |
| **Cost per turn rises without longer contexts**      | Model service   | Prefix-cache hit rate collapsed after a change to the stable prefix             | Cached-token share of input tokens per trajectory                                                                            | Context assembler: restore a stable layout (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging)        |
| **Trajectories busy but going nowhere**              | Harness         | Activity without established task progress                                      | Repeated actions and state as signals, not proof of nonprogress                                                              | Recovery: progress detection (@sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs)                                  |
| **Sandbox leases time out under bursts**             | Sandbox hosts   | Ready reserve exhausted under the configured replenishment and admission policy | Standby empty; queued admissions and restores                                                                                | Isolation envelope: pool sizing (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling)                             |
| **Duplicate external effects after a restart**       | Harness and log | Effects dispatched before their intent was durable, or retried unsettled        | Distinct effect records for one intended operation; dispatch evidence absent from an expected complete authoritative history | Trajectory log and gateway: write-ahead intent and settlement (@sec-vol3-persistence-wal) |
| **A failing dependency drains budgets**              | Tool gateway    | The model retrying a tool whose service is down                                 | Dependency-scoped outcomes and admission/attempt rates                                                                       | Recovery: circuit breaker (@sec-vol3-sagas-containment)                                   |
| **Retrieved facts contradict the workspace**         | Durable stores  | An index or memory entry not invalidated after a source write                   | Version mismatches rejected by the retrieval contract                                                                        | Durable stores: invalidation (@sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation)                          |
| **Spending exceeds limits across a delegation tree** | Fleet           | Children spending from a shared budget without reservations                     | Reserved versus settled spend per tree                                                                                       | Fleet: spending governance (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-governance)                         |

: **Deployment Failure Signals**: The symptom each pool shows when a component is missing or undersized, the signal that exposes it, and the component that responds. {#tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-failures tbl-colwidths="[18,11,23,22,26]"}

## Summary {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-summary}

The reference architecture is the book's argument laid out as a system. One component, the model, proposes. Every other component closes an exposure the proposal creates: the context assembler, serving memory, and durable stores close state; the tool gateway and isolation envelope close authority; the harness, trajectory log, and recovery close horizon; evaluation measures whether the closure held; the learning loop improves the proposer only after evaluation can tell; and the fleet multiplies all of it. A task's H·S·A position selects which components it needs, and a failure's symptom points at the component that should have caught it.
